claims.text: Ultrafast-quenched nanoparticles exhibit greater structural and compositional stability under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions than slower-quenched nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching traps internal strain and a defect-rich microstructure in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Trapped internal strain and defects act as diffusion barriers that hinder atomic rearrangement and phase segregation.
Different quenching rates introduce different levels of internal strain and defect density into FeCoNiCuCr-like nanoparticles.
A quenching-rate range of approximately 10^3 to 10^6 K/s can be used to manipulate the metastable microstructure.
Inert-gas atomization can provide an ultrafast quenching rate of approximately 10^6 K/s for the proposed nanoparticles.
Metastable strain and defect structures created by rapid quenching impede atomic diffusion and grain-boundary migration.
Defects produced by rapid quenching serve as pinning sites.
Diffusion retardation caused by trapped strain and defects suppresses phase segregation and grain growth during high-temperature operation.
Ultrafast-quenched nanoparticles will retain broader XRD peaks after thermal treatment than slower-quenched nanoparticles.
Ultrafast-quenched nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution after thermal treatment than slower-quenched nanoparticles.
Slower-quenched nanoparticles will exhibit noticeable phase segregation and grain growth after thermal treatment.
Slower-quenched nanoparticles have lower internal strain and defect densities than ultrafast-quenched nanoparticles.
Rapid relaxation of metastable features during prolonged high-temperature exposure would limit the proposed stabilization mechanism.
Gas composition can significantly alter diffusion behavior and thereby limit the applicability of the hypothesis.
